name: When Baghdad Taught the World
description: Eight centuries of Islamic history in which scholars from Spain to Persia translated, tested and improved the knowledge of earlier peoples and built cities, mosques and books.

checkpoints.name: The faith and the first caliphs
checkpoints.note: Muhammad received the Quran and founded the community at Medina, and the Islamic calendar counts from his move there. The first four caliphs took the new faith across Arabia and beyond.

checkpoints.name: The Umayyad age
checkpoints.note: From Damascus the Umayyads ruled a vast empire. They raised the Dome of the Rock, minted the Islamic dinar and carried their rule to al-Andalus in Spain.

checkpoints.name: Baghdad rises
checkpoints.note: The Abbasid caliphs built Baghdad. At the House of Wisdom scholars like al-Khwarizmi created algebra and spread the Hindu-Arabic numerals, under Harun al-Rashid the court was famed, and tales that became The Thousand and One Nights were gathered.

checkpoints.name: Cairo, Cordoba and the great minds
checkpoints.note: Rival courts competed for scholars. Cairo got al-Azhar, Cordoba enlarged its great mosque, Ibn al-Haytham wrote on light, Avicenna on medicine and Omar Khayyam on mathematics and poems, astronomers refined the astrolabe, and Ferdowsi composed the Shahnameh.

checkpoints.name: Late brilliance and the Mongol blow
checkpoints.note: Averroes, Maimonides, al-Jazari and Rumi worked in a divided world. The Alhambra rose in Granada and Mongol troops destroyed Baghdad in 1258, yet Ibn Khaldun wrote a new theory of history afterwards.
